title: Builder
summary: Assemble a complex object step by step; keep the product immutable at the end.

parts.rule: A builder collects construction choices under readable method names, validates them, and produces a finished object from build(). The built object should be usable immediately and is usually immutable. The builder may be mutable while assembling values, but that temporary state should not leak into the product.
parts.why: A constructor with many optional positional arguments is easy to call incorrectly and hard to read later. Named builder steps make each choice visible and give cross-field validation one place to run. That convenience costs an extra type and more methods, so it pays off only when construction is genuinely complicated.
parts.example: Suppose Request needs method and URL, with optional headers, body, timeout, and retry count. A call such as new Request("POST", "/reports", null, payload, 2, 3, true) hides what the final four values mean. Instead, RequestBuilder.post("/reports").header("Content-Type", "application/json").body(payload).timeoutSeconds(2).retries(3).build() states each decision. During build(), require a URL, reject a timeout below 1 second, and reject a body on HEAD. Copy the header map so later builder changes cannot mutate the Request. The result contains method=POST, timeout=2, and retries=3 as immutable fields. A test can also build a minimal GET with only method and URL. If the same product has a required sequence, the API can expose stages: start() returns a NeedsUrl step; url() returns a Ready step; only Ready has build(). That prevents an invalid half-built request at compile time in languages with expressive types. Compare this with a simple Point(x, y): two required coordinates are already clear, so PointBuilder would add ceremony without removing ambiguity.
parts.use: Use a builder for objects with several independent options, cross-field validation, or a required assembly order. Common examples are HTTP requests, queries, test fixtures, and configuration objects. Keep required values obvious, validate once in build(), and return a product that no longer depends on the builder.
parts.refuse: Prefer a constructor or an options record when there are only two or three clear fields. Do not let build() return an invalid object that needs more setters. Avoid reusing one mutable builder across threads, and do not make callers retain the builder as the real domain object. The pattern should clarify construction, not hide it.

body:
Rule. A builder collects construction choices under readable method names, validates them, and produces a finished object from build(). The built object should be usable immediately and is usually immutable. The builder may be mutable while assembling values, but that temporary state should not leak into the product.

Why it matters. A constructor with many optional positional arguments is easy to call incorrectly and hard to read later. Named builder steps make each choice visible and give cross-field validation one place to run. That convenience costs an extra type and more methods, so it pays off only when construction is genuinely complicated.

Worked example. Suppose Request needs method and URL, with optional headers, body, timeout, and retry count. A call such as new Request("POST", "/reports", null, payload, 2, 3, true) hides what the final four values mean. Instead, RequestBuilder.post("/reports").header("Content-Type", "application/json").body(payload).timeoutSeconds(2).retries(3).build() states each decision. During build(), require a URL, reject a timeout below 1 second, and reject a body on HEAD. Copy the header map so later builder changes cannot mutate the Request. The result contains method=POST, timeout=2, and retries=3 as immutable fields. A test can also build a minimal GET with only method and URL. If the same product has a required sequence, the API can expose stages: start() returns a NeedsUrl step; url() returns a Ready step; only Ready has build(). That prevents an invalid half-built request at compile time in languages with expressive types. Compare this with a simple Point(x, y): two required coordinates are already clear, so PointBuilder would add ceremony without removing ambiguity.

[[diagram:steps]]

When to use. Use a builder for objects with several independent options, cross-field validation, or a required assembly order. Common examples are HTTP requests, queries, test fixtures, and configuration objects. Keep required values obvious, validate once in build(), and return a product that no longer depends on the builder.

When to refuse. Prefer a constructor or an options record when there are only two or three clear fields. Do not let build() return an invalid object that needs more setters. Avoid reusing one mutable builder across threads, and do not make callers retain the builder as the real domain object. The pattern should clarify construction, not hide it.
